invariants.title: Composition depth
invariants.body:
The axis `src/components/` splits on — **how many other public components a
component composes**, never UI purpose. Purpose grouping is Storybook's job
(`Form/Controls`, `Overlays`, `Actions`, …), so one folder holds components from
several Storybook sections and that is correct.

| Term | Composes | Exported | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **base** | at most `TrustyIcon` | yes | `TrustyButton`, `TrustyTextInput`, `TrustyDialog`, `TrustyTree` |
| **specialized** | exactly one other component, with fixed non-configurable content | yes | `TrustyBarChart`, `TrustyLineChart`, `TrustyThumbnail` |
| **form** | the label/error/submit contract itself | yes | `TrustyForm`, `TrustyFormItem` |
| **composite** | two or more public components, no app or domain logic | yes | `TrustyCodeBlock`, `TrustyContextMenu`, `TrustyDropdownMenu` |
| **private** | shared internals a public component wraps | **no** | `AlertBase`, `CodeEditorBase`, `DialogBase`, `EditableBase`, `NumberFieldBase`, `TagBase`, `TextInputBase` |

**Where a component may not go:** anything that knows about app domain,
runtime, or backend state belongs in the consuming app, not here. `trusty-ui`
imports no other local package.

invariants.title: The three form layers
invariants.body:
Form components stack in three layers, each owning exactly one concern, each
usable alone. The layer names are the vocabulary; see the README for the
composition examples.

| Layer | Term | Owns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **control** | the bare widget — no label, no error text |
| 2 | **field** (`TrustyFormItem`) | label, hint, error, required marker, and every ARIA link between them |
| 3 | **form** (`TrustyForm`) | the `<form novalidate>`, field spacing, error summary, actions, `submit` |

A control carries no chrome: it takes `invalid` and `required`, and lets
everything else (`id`, `aria-describedby`, `v-model`, …) fall through to its
focusable element. A field feeds it those attributes through the `field` object
on its default scoped slot.

**Validation is the consumer's.** No layer validates anything — the app owns the
v-models and decides what counts as an error, which is what keeps the library
validation-library-agnostic.

invariants.title: Token tiers
invariants.body:
Two tiers in `src/styles/tokens/`, and components may only see one of them.

- **primitive** (`primitives.css`) — the raw palette, all oklch,
  `--color-kaki-500`. Never referenced outside the semantic tier.
- **semantic** (`semantic.css`) — the design system's public API:
  `--color-primary-highlight`, `--color-text`, `--space-*`, `--radius-*`,
  `--duration-*`. This file is the canonical token reference.
  Every colour role is a `light-dark()` pair; `:root` declares
  `color-scheme: light dark`, and an app pins a mode by overriding it.
  Decorative colour gets roles too: `--color-tag-*` for tag hues. Chart series
  are the exception, component-level `--trusty-chart-series-*` that ChartBase
  owns, since nothing outside a chart draws them.

Components style through semantic tokens only; `token-tiers.spec.ts` fails when
a component's source names a primitive. Cascade layers run
`reset, tokens, base`, assigned by `main.css`; layered styles lose to unlayered
ones, so scoped SFC styles and app CSS win without specificity games.

invariants.title: Two stylesheets
invariants.body:
| Sheet | Holds | Loading |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@louislp/trusty-ui/src/styles/main.css` | reset, tokens, base element styles, the Fontsource `@font-face` imports | the app imports it once at its entry |
| `@louislp/trusty-ui/style.css` | the components' own bundled rules | automatic — the built entry imports it |

The global sheet restyles the consumer's own document, so the app decides when
that happens. Skipping it is the classic failure: components render with layout
and structure intact and every `var(--…)` unresolved.

invariants.title: Icons
invariants.body:
- **Iconify icon** — every icon is a `collection:icon` name; the library's own
  are Phosphor regular (`ph:*`), browsable at https://icon-sets.iconify.design/.
  `TrustyIconName` is `` `${string}:${string}` ``, so a bare name fails
  `type-check` instead of rendering nothing; it is not a union of real names,
  which `vue-tsc` cannot reduce at Iconify's size (`TS2590`). The icons the
  components use are bundled and render offline. Any other name is fetched from
  the Iconify API on first render. `@iconify/vue` is a peer dependency, so an
  app's own `addCollection` / `addAPIProvider` reaches every `<TrustyIcon>`.

invariants.title: Code highlighting
invariants.body:
`TrustyCodeLanguage` is the union of languages the code components can label and
highlight. Widening it means adding a grammar loader, not just a string.

invariants.title: The single entry
invariants.body:
`src/index.ts` is the entire public surface: the four category barrels plus
the `TrustyIconName` type. Category folders and
`src/internal/` are internal organization, so there are
deliberately no per-category subpath exports — every component is imported from `@louislp/trusty-ui`
itself. The `style.css`, `styles/*`, and `fonts/*` subpaths exist for one reason
only — CSS and font files cannot travel through a JS entry.

components.name: TrustyCodeBlock
components.summary: A multi-line code surface: a header with the language label and a copy-to-clipboard button, above the code with a line-number gutter in a two-axis scroll area.
useWhen: showing a multi-line snippet the user may want to read or copy: payloads, configs, logs.
letting the user correct that snippet in place — set `editable`.
dontUseFor: a short inline reference (a file name, a property) inside running text: use a plain
a single line of free text or an identifier in a form: use `TrustyTextInput`.
prose in a form: use `TrustyTextInput` — the mono font and gutter are wrong for sentences.
components.description:
A multi-line code surface: a header with the language label and a copy-to-clipboard
button, above the code with a line-number gutter in a two-axis scroll area.
Setting `language` also syntax-highlights the code via Shiki (Ayu Mirage theme,
loaded lazily); omit it for plain preformatted text.

Read-only by default. Set `editable` and the header gains an **Edit** button:
pressing it swaps the code for a CodeMirror editor — same grammars and theme, so
the colours don't shift — and replaces Edit with **Save**. The language label
becomes a ghost select, collapsed until clicked, so the user can switch the
grammar while editing. It opens on the `language` prop, falling back to JSON
when that is omitted. Save commits the draft, returns to the read view, and fires
`submit` with the new code and language. Bind `v-model:code` (and
`v-model:language`) to have the edit written back to your own state as well; a
plain `:code` / `:language` binding still updates what's displayed. The draft — code and
language alike — is local until Save, so an abandoned edit emits nothing.

While editing, **Tab** indents by two spaces and **Shift+Tab** outdents; **Esc then
Tab** leaves the editor, since Tab no longer moves focus. CodeMirror loads on
first edit from its own chunk, so a consumer who never sets `editable` never
ships it.

Constrain the height from outside (`max-block-size` on the component) to make
long code scroll; unconstrained, the block grows with its content.

**Use it when**
- showing a multi-line snippet the user may want to read or copy: payloads, configs, logs.
- letting the user correct that snippet in place — set `editable`.

**Don't use it for**
- a short inline reference (a file name, a property) inside running text: use a plain
  `<code>` element — the base stylesheet styles it on the design system.
- a single line of free text or an identifier in a form: use `TrustyTextInput`.
- prose in a form: use `TrustyTextInput` — the mono font and gutter are wrong for sentences.

components.name: TrustyFilterTag
components.summary: A tag chip that switches on and off.
useWhen: offering a row of filter or facet chips over a list, a log, or a canvas.
toggling a view option that reads as a label rather than a control: "errors", "archived", "mine".
dontUseFor: attaching or detaching a tag on an entity — a chip whose click means add or remove: use TrustyTag
a status or state you only read, never click: use TrustyBadge
collecting a list of tags in a form: use TrustyTagInput
a toggle that reads as a control rather than a tag, or one that needs an icon: use TrustyToggle, or TrustyToggleGroup for a mutually exclusive set
components.description:
A tag chip that switches on and off. Same seven decorative hues as `TrustyTag`, no glyph, and a ring while it is on — clicking flips `v-model` and `aria-pressed` with it, so assistive tech reads the chip as a toggle button. Nothing is added or destroyed by a click; the chip only says whether its facet is currently on.

Each chip owns one boolean. A row of them is a plain `v-for` over the app's facets — there is no group component, because the app already holds the shape of its filter state.

**Use it when**
- offering a row of filter or facet chips over a list, a log, or a canvas.
- toggling a view option that reads as a label rather than a control: "errors", "archived", "mine".

**Don't use it for**
- attaching or detaching a tag on an entity — a chip whose click means add or remove: use TrustyTag
- a status or state you only read, never click: use TrustyBadge
- collecting a list of tags in a form: use TrustyTagInput
- a toggle that reads as a control rather than a tag, or one that needs an icon: use TrustyToggle, or TrustyToggleGroup for a mutually exclusive set

components.name: TrustyKeyboardBadge
components.summary: A small badge showing a keyboard shortcut as one key-cap chip per key.
useWhen: hinting at a shortcut next to a command: a menu row, a tooltip, a help page.
dontUseFor: status or category labels — that's TrustyBadge.
components.description:
A small badge showing a keyboard shortcut as one key-cap chip per key. 'mod' renders the platform's primary modifier (⌘ on Apple, Ctrl elsewhere) — prefer it over 'cmd'/'ctrl' for cross-platform shortcuts. Named special keys ('cmd', 'shift', 'up', …) always render their own symbol; text keys render literally ('D', 'F2', 'Esc'). The key type is a closed union (no free-form strings) — extend TrustyKeyboardKey when a key is missing. Purely visual — it never listens for the keys itself; whoever renders it owns the actual key handling.

**Use it when**
- hinting at a shortcut next to a command: a menu row, a tooltip, a help page.

**Don't use it for**
- status or category labels — that's TrustyBadge.

props.name: keys
props.description: Keys of the shortcut, in press order. `mod` renders the platform's primary modifier (⌘ on Apple, Ctrl elsewhere), named special keys render their glyph (`['mod', 'shift', 'D']` → ⌘ ⇧ D), and text keys render literally. A closed set: extend `TrustyKeyboardKey` when a key is missing. Display-only — key handling stays with the consumer.

stories.description: A single text key.

stories.name: NamedKeys

components.summary: Old-timey ad emphasis rays, alternating seiji and kaki, with a hand-drawn "line boil": three jittered redraws of the same rays swap on a stepped ~3 fps cycle,…
useWhen: a badge, stamp or status chip wants a burst over it (`stamp`)
a card or hero edge wants rays shooting off it (`burst`)
a display heading wants a comic emphasis ping beside it (`spark`)
dontUseFor: anything that carries meaning: it is hidden from assistive tech, so say it in text, or use TrustyBadge
showing that work is running: use TrustySpinner
an icon in a control: use TrustyIcon
dense product UI: one per view, on a marketing or empty-state surface, or it stops reading as emphasis
components.description:
Old-timey ad emphasis rays, alternating seiji and kaki, with a hand-drawn "line boil": three jittered redraws of the same rays swap on a stepped ~3 fps cycle, so the mark reads as drawn rather than rendered. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` it holds still on the first frame.

It is pure ornament — `aria-hidden`, no text, no interaction. It has no size of its own: set `inline-size` on it, and `rotate` or `scale: -1 1` to point it the other way.

**Use it when**
- a badge, stamp or status chip wants a burst over it (`stamp`)
- a card or hero edge wants rays shooting off it (`burst`)
- a display heading wants a comic emphasis ping beside it (`spark`)

**Don't use it for**
- anything that carries meaning: it is hidden from assistive tech, so say it in text, or use TrustyBadge
- showing that work is running: use TrustySpinner
- an icon in a control: use TrustyIcon
- dense product UI: one per view, on a marketing or empty-state surface, or it stops reading as emphasis

components.name: TrustyTable
components.summary: Rows and columns as a real HTML table, so a screen reader announces the grid and the headers that name each cell.
useWhen: records share a set of fields and the user compares them across rows.
dontUseFor: laying a page out in rows and columns: that is CSS grid's job, not a table's
hierarchical or nested records: use TrustyTree
a list of one field per record: use TrustyTree, or plain markup
picking one value from many: use TrustySelect
components.description:
Rows and columns as a real HTML table, so a screen reader announces the grid and the headers that name each cell. Columns are declared once and every row supplies its cells by key; a cell is text, text with a quieter second line, or whatever a 'cell-<key>' slot renders. It optionally carries row selection, sortable headers, and a footer housing TrustyPagination and a status line.

The table shows the data it is given and never reorders or slices it — sorting and paging are reported through v-model so the data source can apply them, which is what lets the same component page through 10 rows or 10,000.

**Use it when**
- records share a set of fields and the user compares them across rows.

**Don't use it for**
- laying a page out in rows and columns: that is CSS grid's job, not a table's
- hierarchical or nested records: use TrustyTree
- a list of one field per record: use TrustyTree, or plain markup
- picking one value from many: use TrustySelect

components.summary: A clickable tag chip: a short label in one of seven decorative hues, carrying one glyph that says what clicking it does — a leading `+` to add it, or a…
useWhen: letting someone attach or detach keywords, categories or labels on an entity.
dontUseFor: a chip that switches on and off rather than adding or removing anything — a row of filter chips: use TrustyFilterTag
a status or state you only read, never click: use TrustyBadge
collecting a list of tags in a form: use TrustyTagInput, which owns the field, the keyboard editing and the v-model

A clickable tag chip: a short label in one of seven decorative hues, carrying one glyph that says what clicking it does — a leading `+` to add it, or a trailing `×` to remove it, never both. The hues mean nothing on their own; the app decides what "purple" stands for.

Every click means the same thing, so the tag holds no state of its own: it emits `click` and the app changes its list.

**Use it when**
- letting someone attach or detach keywords, categories or labels on an entity.

**Don't use it for**
- a chip that switches on and off rather than adding or removing anything — a row of filter chips: use TrustyFilterTag
- a status or state you only read, never click: use TrustyBadge
- collecting a list of tags in a form: use TrustyTagInput, which owns the field, the keyboard editing and the v-model
- a general-purpose action: use TrustyButton

components.name: TrustyBarChart
components.summary: Categories along the x-axis, one bar per series in each.
useWhen: you are comparing up to five series across as many categories as you need
the values are magnitudes read against a zero baseline
dontUseFor: a trend or a shape across ordered categories: use TrustyLineChart
a grid of records the user sorts or selects: use TrustyTable
a single progress value: that is a readout, use TrustyBadge
components.description:
Categories along the x-axis, one bar per series in each. Chart.js paints the plot; the component draws the panel around it — title, description, legend — and keeps a visually hidden table of the same numbers for assistive tech. Hover a value for a TrustyHoverCard; Chart.js does not draw its own tooltip. Hovering also fades every other bar to 40% opacity, so the one under the pointer reads as the focus.

The chart fills its parent, so give the parent a width and a height (or take the 16rem floor). Bars keep their `size` thickness rather than shrinking, so the plot claims the width its clusters need and a narrow parent should scroll — give that scrolling parent `tabindex="0"`, or it is unreachable by keyboard.

Pass at most five series: that is how many colours the palette has, and past five they repeat (with a development warning). A short `values` array or an explicit `null` is a gap, not a zero — no bar, a break in the line, and an empty cell in the table. Categories have no cap. **Dismissing depends on the severity.** If the user can simply ignore the notice or resolve it themselves, they may close it; if it reports a system problem they cannot act on — "connection lost" — it stays until the condition does.

components.description:
A markdown field: the formatting bar on top of a surface that **styles the
markdown as it is typed**. One value — the markdown source — and no preview
pane. The styling *is* the preview, which is why nothing here renders HTML and
the library ships no markdown renderer: what you store is what the consumer
renders, however it likes.

**The markers are concealed until the caret reaches them.** A heading shows no
`#`, `**bold**` reads as **bold**, a link shows its label and not its target,
and a fenced block shows neither fence — until the caret lands there, and what it
landed on becomes editable source again.

How much comes back is the width of what the marker describes. A **block**
marker is its line — click anywhere on a heading, a quote or a list item and its
own syntax reveals, however long the line and wherever on it the caret sits. An
**inline** marker is one run inside the line, so only the run you click into
reveals: put the caret in the one bold word of a paragraph and just its `**`
come back, while the rest of the line keeps reading as prose. Nested runs come
back together, since `**_both_**` is one place. A fenced block reveals as a
whole, its fences being lines of their own.

A field nobody is editing shows no markers at all: revealing follows the caret
only while the field has focus, so a blurred editor never sits there displaying
the line its caret was last left on.

Nothing is ever rewritten to achieve this — the document is exactly what you
typed, and `v-model` never fires on a caret move. Only what is *drawn* changes.

Quotes and fenced code are drawn as **bands** — one tinted box around the *whole
run*, its rounding and its outer edges only on the rows that open and close it —
so three quoted lines read as one block instead of three stacked boxes. A quote
carries a single spine down its leading edge; a fenced block sits inside a full
frame, on the one surface in the field darker than the field itself. A block
taller than the field scrolls with the field, which is the only scroller the
surface has: see `maxRows`. Headings scale, emphasis stacks (`**_both_**` is bold
*and* italic), and code holds no emphasis at all.

**A line break opens a gap; wrapping does not.** Every block edge — a heading
giving way to its paragraph, one paragraph to the next, a paragraph to a quote or
a list — opens a half-gap on each side of itself, so blocks stand off each other
instead of running together. Press Enter and you have started a second paragraph,
and it is spaced off the first. A paragraph that merely *wraps* stays packed
however tall it grows, because it is still one paragraph. Bands and lists are
packed too: their lines are lines of one thing, and a gap between two quoted
lines or two items would say otherwise.

A **band** takes its gap differently, because its tint covers its own padding:
the air that separates it from the block above and below is carried entirely by
those blocks, and what is inside the tint is the band's own breathing room. So a
quote stands off its neighbours by a full gap and still has room around the words
in it.

List markers are the one thing left on screen — concealing them would take the
list's shape with them — and items hang a step to the leading edge of the prose,
so a run of them reads as a list rather than as short paragraphs. A number is already the thing it means and is
left alone; a bulleted item's `-`, `*` or `+` is *drawn* as a **•**, and hands
its own character back when the caret lands on the line. Nesting is the source's
own indentation, which is why only the one marker character is ever swapped. A
thematic break (`---`, `***` or `___`) draws the rule itself, and shows its
dashes again when the caret lands on the line.

**A link opens on ⌘- or Ctrl-click**, or with ⌘/Ctrl+Enter from the caret, in a
new tab — a plain click still has to mean "put the caret here" while the field is
being edited, so it does not open one. In a disabled field there is no caret to
place and a plain click opens. The target is the element's tooltip, so a label
that hides its URL can still be checked before it is followed. Only
`http`, `https`, `mailto` and `tel` targets open: the document is user input,
so a `javascript:` target is drawn as a link and does nothing.

**The bar reflects the caret.** Move it into a quoted, bolded word and both
segments press; move it out and both release. Linking stays dimmed until
something is selected, because a link needs a label.

**Every action has a shortcut**, and it is the one the bar announces — ⌘B or
Ctrl+B for bold, either modifier, on any platform. Enter continues a list or a
quote and counts a numbered list on; Enter on an empty item ends the list. **Tab
nests a list item** and Shift+Tab lifts it back out — by the width of the item's
own marker, which is the column a child has to reach to be one. Off a list, and
at the outer level of one going backwards, Tab moves focus the way it does in any
other field: a field a keyboard cannot leave is a trap.

The bar is chrome, not part of the field: hover and focus light the **text area**
alone, and clicking the bar does not take focus off the text, so the selection
survives the press. A format toggle is one undo step.

`rows` and `maxRows` bound the text area in real lines — it grows as it is
typed into, and scrolls once it hits `maxRows`. The scroller is CodeMirror's
own, deliberately, and not a `TrustyScrollArea`: the editor renders only the
lines in view and measures them against its own element, so a scroll container
outside it would report the wrong viewport and it would draw the wrong lines.

**Use it when**
- a field holds prose the user should be able to format — a description, a
  comment, release notes, a report
- you want markdown *stored*, and the formatting shown while it is written
- the field belongs in a form: wrap it in `TrustyFormItem` for its label, hint
  and error, exactly like `TrustyTextInput`

**Don't use it for**
- plain unformatted text — use `TrustyTextInput`, or `TrustyEditableText` for
  edit-in-place
- source code — use `TrustyCodeBlock`, which labels the language, highlights it
  with Shiki, and offers a line-number gutter
- rendering markdown that is already written — this component only edits; render
  the stored source in the consuming app
- a full rich-text document with tables, images and embeds — that is a different
  component, and a different editor engine

**Under it:** CodeMirror 6, dynamically imported so it never reaches a bundle
that does not mount the field ([ADR 0001](https://github.com/LouisLP/trusty-ui/blob/main/docs/adr/0001-codemirror-for-code-editing.md)).
No markdown grammar package: the rules are a scanner of pure string functions
(`TrustyMarkdownEditor.markdown.ts`), which is also what the bar's pressed state
and the keyboard shortcuts read.

**A contenteditable, not a `<textarea>`** — the same consequence
`TrustyCodeBlock`'s editor carries: `required` is advisory (`aria-required`) and
the value does not take part in native form submission. The `v-model` is the
value, which is how every Trusty UI form already works.

components.name: TrustyAccordion

dontUseFor: one standalone collapsible area inside another component — no surface, no group behaviour: use TrustyCollapsible
swapping one region between peer views, where exactly one is always visible: use TrustyTabs
content the user always needs: keep it outside the accordion
components.description:
A vertically stacked set of collapsible panels on their own surface.

Each item's `value` names both what `v-model` reports and the slot that fills that panel's body. The item's `label` and `icon` render in the header; the body is the item's `description` followed by that slot, and nothing else — so an item that is only prose needs no slot, and an item that is only controls needs no description.

`single` (the default) keeps at most one panel open and lets you close it again; `multiple` reports an array. Every header is a `<button>` inside an `<h3>`: Space and Enter toggle, arrow keys walk the headers, Home and End jump to the ends.

**Use it when**
- several related groups share one surface and not all of them need to be visible at once: settings categories, parameter groups, configuration sections.

**Don't use it for**
- one standalone collapsible area inside another component — no surface, no group behaviour: use TrustyCollapsible
- swapping one region between peer views, where exactly one is always visible: use TrustyTabs
- content the user always needs: keep it outside the accordion

components.name: TrustyCard
components.summary: A static surface that groups related content under a heading.

several pieces of content share one header row that carries the actions for all of them
dontUseFor: a group the user can fold away: use TrustyCollapsible, or TrustyAccordion for several of them
a message about the current screen: use TrustyBanner, or TrustyAlert when the user must respond
switching between panels of content: use TrustyTabs

the label, hint, and error wiring around a single control: that is TrustyFormItem's job, and it belongs *inside* the card's body
components.description:
A static surface that groups related content under a heading. It draws the panel — surface, radius, padding, the rhythm between header and body — and nothing else: the card has no behaviour, no state, and no interaction of its own.

Three places to put content:

| Where | What goes there |
| --- | --- |
| `title` / `description` | the heading (an `<h3>`) and one line of prose about the group |
| `actions` slot | controls acting on the whole group, pinned to the end of the header row |
| default slot | the body — form controls, a table, a read-out, whatever the group is |

A titled card names its own `<section>` through `aria-labelledby`, which makes it a region assistive tech can jump to. An untitled one stays an anonymous `<section>` and adds no landmark noise.

The card sizes to its container: give it a width in your layout (a grid column, a flex track) rather than expecting one here.

**Use it when**
- a group of related controls or read-outs needs boxing off under a heading (a parameter block, a settings group, an inspector panel)
- several pieces of content share one header row that carries the actions for all of them

**Don't use it for**
- a group the user can fold away: use TrustyCollapsible, or TrustyAccordion for several of them
- a message about the current screen: use TrustyBanner, or TrustyAlert when the user must respond
- switching between panels of content: use TrustyTabs
- content that floats above the page: use TrustyPopover, TrustyHoverCard, or TrustyDialog
- the label, hint, and error wiring around a single control: that is TrustyFormItem's job, and it belongs *inside* the card's body

components.name: TrustyCollapsible
components.summary: One collapsible area, for use inside another component — a group of related inputs, form fields, or settings that need not be visible by default.
useWhen: one group of related inputs, fields, or settings inside another component need not be visible by default.
several such areas must open and close independently of one another.
dontUseFor: a stack of panels on their own surface where at most one should stand open: use TrustyAccordion
content the user must see to finish the task: revealing it is one click they may never make
components.description:
One collapsible area, for use inside another component — a group of related inputs, form fields, or settings that need not be visible by default. It brings no surface of its own and knows nothing about siblings, so it drops into whatever panel hosts it and several of them open independently.

The `description` is the trigger's text; the default slot holds the revealed content. The header is a `<button>`, so Space and Enter toggle it, and the marker turns from right to down as it opens.

Leave `open` unbound to let it manage itself, or bind `v-model:open` to drive it from outside — including to start it open.

**Use it when**
- one group of related inputs, fields, or settings inside another component need not be visible by default.
- several such areas must open and close independently of one another.

**Don't use it for**
- a stack of panels on their own surface where at most one should stand open: use TrustyAccordion
- content the user must see to finish the task: revealing it is one click they may never make

props.name: description
props.description: The trigger's text, and its accessible name.

stories.name: Disabled

stories.name: Stacked

content that should size to its container instead of scrolling: fix the layout first
making a very long list cheap to render: this styles scrollbars, it does not virtualize

A scroll container with design-system scrollbars that reveal on hover or scroll, then fade out. Pick vertical, horizontal, or both (vertical by default).

**Use it when**
- a panel scrolls and native scrollbars would look heavy or inconsistent across platforms.

**Don't use it for**
- the page itself: the document's own scrollbar is the right one there
- content that should size to its container instead of scrolling: fix the layout first
- making a very long list cheap to render: this styles scrollbars, it does not virtualize

components.description:
A one- or two-pixel rule that divides content, horizontally or vertically. It carries `role="separator"` so screen readers announce the split.

A vertical separator has no height of its own — it stretches to its flex parent, so give that parent a height.

**Use it when**
- two groups sit adjacent and need a visible break between them: menu sections, toolbar clusters, stacked rows.

**Don't use it for**
- spacing: reach for the --space-* tokens instead
- an edge on a surface: give the surface its own border
- splitting regions the user can resize: use TrustySplitter

stories.name: InAToolbar

a stack of sections that open and close rather than resize: use TrustyAccordion

Resizable panels: place TrustySplitterPanels in the default slot and the drag handles between them appear automatically. Lay it out horizontally or vertically. Give it a storage key and the layout survives reloads (make the key unique per splitter; a saved layout wins over defaultSize).

**Don't use it for**
- regions at fixed or purely responsive sizes: lay them out with CSS grid or flex
- a stack of sections that open and close rather than resize: use TrustyAccordion
- one region that only needs to scroll: use TrustyScrollArea

components.name: TrustyIcon
components.summary: Renders any Iconify icon, named in collection:icon form ('ph:house').
useWhen: a glyph needs to appear on its own, outside any component that already takes an icon name.
dontUseFor: an icon inside a component that has an icon prop (TrustyButton, TrustyToggle, TrustyTabs and friends): pass the name, don't nest one
a clickable glyph: use TrustyButton with 'icon' and no label, paired with an aria-label
status next to text: use TrustyBadge
components.description:
Renders any Iconify icon, named in collection:icon form ('ph:house'). The library defaults to Phosphor regular ('ph:*'); browse names at https://icon-sets.iconify.design/. The icons the library's own components use are bundled and render offline; any other name is fetched from the Iconify API on first render. Give it a token size, or omit 'size' and it renders at 1em, tracking the surrounding text.

**Use it when**
- a glyph needs to appear on its own, outside any component that already takes an icon name.

**Don't use it for**
- an icon inside a component that has an icon prop (TrustyButton, TrustyToggle, TrustyTabs and friends): pass the name, don't nest one
- a clickable glyph: use TrustyButton with 'icon' and no label, paired with an aria-label
- status next to text: use TrustyBadge

props.name: name
props.description: Iconify name in `collection:icon` form (`ph:house`). The names the library's own components use are bundled and render offline; any other is fetched from the Iconify API.

props.name: size
props.description: Fixed design-token size (styled via `[data-size]` in CSS). Omit to size at `1em`, so the icon tracks the font-size of surrounding text.

stories.name: Bundled

stories.name: Iconify

components.name: TrustyNavigationTabs
components.summary: A vertical rail of tabs that stands beside the region it drives — the settings-dialog sidebar, the tool toolbar.
useWhen: a persistent sidebar swaps a large content region beside it, like a settings dialog
an icon rail picks the active tool or view and stays on screen while you work
dontUseFor: an inline strip above the region it swaps: use TrustyTabs, which runs horizontally too
items that are real destinations and change the URL: use plain links, so they can be middle-clicked, copied and land fresh
a value the user sets rather than a view they switch to: use TrustyToggleGroup
groups that may all stand open at once: use TrustyAccordion
hierarchical content: use TrustyTree
components.description:
A vertical rail of tabs that stands beside the region it drives — the settings-dialog sidebar, the tool toolbar. Always vertical, so arrow keys run up and down. The active tab takes a filled wash and a bar on the rail's outer edge, which is what makes it read as a place you are rather than a control you pressed. Each tab's 'value' doubles as the name of the slot holding its panel; leave the slot out and you get a rail-only strip you drive externally through v-model.

It is the same machinery as TrustyTabs — same Reka primitive, same tab semantics — dressed as a navigation rail. Reach for it when the strip is the frame around the content rather than a control inside it.

**Use it when**
- a persistent sidebar swaps a large content region beside it, like a settings dialog
- an icon rail picks the active tool or view and stays on screen while you work

**Don't use it for**
- an inline strip above the region it swaps: use TrustyTabs, which runs horizontally too
- items that are real destinations and change the URL: use plain links, so they can be middle-clicked, copied and land fresh
- a value the user sets rather than a view they switch to: use TrustyToggleGroup
- groups that may all stand open at once: use TrustyAccordion
- hierarchical content: use TrustyTree

components.description:
A page strip for a paged list: jump-to-first and previous arrows, the numbered pages around the current one, then next and jump-to-last. It counts in items, not pages — give it the collection's 'total' and how many fit on a page, and it works the page count out. Pages beyond the window collapse into an ellipsis, and the first and last page stay pinned so the ends are always one click away.

**Use it when**
- a list is served one page at a time and the user picks which page to see.

**Don't use it for**
- a list that grows as the user scrolls: there are no pages to name, so render nothing
- stepping through a sequence of form steps: use TrustyTabs
- paging the rows of a table: use TrustyTable, which houses this in its footer

components.name: TrustyStepper

a form is long enough to break into stages the user submits at the end

paging through a list of results: use TrustyPagination
a single yes/no stage, or one that fits on one screen: just show the form
a read-only status timeline nobody navigates: render a plain list
components.description:
Progress through a task that runs over several steps. Each step shows its number — or an icon — with a title and an optional description, and 'v-model' carries the step the user is on, 1-based. By default progress is linear: only the steps already reached and the one straight after can be picked, and the rest read as locked. The strip shows progress and moves between steps; the content of each step lives outside the component, keyed off 'v-model'.

**Use it when**
- one task splits into ordered steps and the user needs to see where they are and how much is left
- a form is long enough to break into stages the user submits at the end

**Don't use it for**
- peer views the user flips between in any order: use TrustyTabs
- paging through a list of results: use TrustyPagination
- a single yes/no stage, or one that fits on one screen: just show the form
- a read-only status timeline nobody navigates: render a plain list

- `icon`: icon name (Iconify `collection:icon`, e.g. `ph:gear`) shown in place of the number
- `disabled`: this step can never be reached, whatever the progress
- `warning`: yellow dot on the indicator — something here needs attention

components.name: TrustyTree
components.summary: A nested tree of selectable rows.
useWhen: navigating hierarchical content (folders, task structures, variable scopes) where one row at a time is the working selection
the hierarchy is the user's to rearrange — 'draggable' reorders and re-parents rows in place
dontUseFor: flat options: use TrustySelect, or TrustyRadioGroup for a short list
reordering a flat list: use TrustyTable, whose rows carry no hierarchy to re-parent into
a few peer views: use TrustyTabs
selecting several rows at once: 'v-model' holds exactly one row's id
components.description:
A nested tree of selectable rows. Parents expand/collapse on click (or ←/→), rows select on click / Enter / Space, and ↑/↓ move focus — all from Reka's Tree primitive. 'v-model' holds the selected row's id, 'v-model:expanded' the ids of open parents. The selected row's group — its parent and siblings — tints as the active branch. Each item can carry color 'tags', shown right-aligned at the end of its row.

Set 'draggable' and rows reorder: drag one onto another row's top or bottom quarter to drop it before or after, onto the middle to nest it inside — or move the focused row with Ctrl/⌘ + Shift + ↑↓←→, so the reorder has a keyboard path too. Rows that model 'children' (an empty array counts) accept nesting; leaves do not, and nothing can be dropped into its own subtree. Bind the rows with 'v-model:items' and the tree applies the reorder itself; bind them as a plain 'items' prop and the 'move' event ('{ id, targetId, position }') is yours to apply — 'moveTreeItem(items, move)', the same pure helper the component uses, is exported for that.

Rows also emit 'row-contextmenu' with the row that was right-clicked, so one surrounding 'TrustyContextMenu' can serve the whole tree — the native right-click still bubbles out to it, which is why the event is not called 'contextmenu'.

**Use it when**
- navigating hierarchical content (folders, task structures, variable scopes) where one row at a time is the working selection
- the hierarchy is the user's to rearrange — 'draggable' reorders and re-parents rows in place

**Don't use it for**
- flat options: use TrustySelect, or TrustyRadioGroup for a short list
- reordering a flat list: use TrustyTable, whose rows carry no hierarchy to re-parent into
- a few peer views: use TrustyTabs
- selecting several rows at once: 'v-model' holds exactly one row's id
